brief.summary: Naren's current research closely mirrors the role: a Simulink-to-Python pipeline, physics-based features, and an early-warning model for bus voltage collapse validated in closed loop. The main risks are how well the results generalize (one held-out bus, perfect scores), thin power-systems depth beyond this one project, and RL experience that so far lies outside the grid domain.
strengths: Direct match to the core duties: built a 13-step pipeline from Simulink simulation to ML training, with 992 physics-based features (grid-wide aggregates, ring-adjacent imbalances, lags, rolling statistics) from 80 base signals.

Evaluates in the terms the JD names: 96% recall, zero false alarms and a 30-second lead time on a held-out bus, plus closed-loop validation where all 10 buses survived after shedding the affected bus to 30% load.

Covers many preferred qualifications: RL with custom reward design (smart greenhouse, IoU-based object localization), ESP32 and IoT sensing, model-integrity work on safety-critical ML (CleanSight), SQL/NoSQL databases, and publications.
gaps: Results rest on a single held-out bus with 100% precision and 1.0 AUC. An interviewer will probe data leakage, how scenarios and faults were split, and whether the model generalizes to other topologies or fault types, especially with 992 features built from lags and rolling windows.

RL experience is in object detection and a greenhouse, not power systems. The JD wants RL prototypes for load shedding, so expect questions on state, action and reward design, safety constraints, and sim-to-real risk.

Education and timeline: the MS began in Winter 2026 with expected completion in Jan. 2028, against a 'near completion' requirement, and the Research Assistant role is listed as starting Sep. 2026 and running to 'Present'. Be ready to clarify dates, availability and how much of the work was independent versus advisor-guided.

eval.better_answer: I'm Naren, a master's student at University of Michigan-Dearborn. What draws me to this role is my current research on AI-based thermal derating and load shedding for DC microgrids. I'm alternating MATLAB/Simulink electrical simulations with a Python ML pipeline—exactly the bridge the role describes. The combination of rigorous simulation validation and ML rigor excites me.

relevance.note: Addresses topology and feature engineering but conflates numbers (512 vs 992 features), omits validation approach, lead time, and recall metrics that define success for this role.

strengths: Correctly identifies ring topology rationale and articulates why circuit-topology resilience matters for the grid.
Recognizes feature engineering as a critical design decision and attempts to explain the pipeline flow (simulation → features → model).
improvements: State the correct feature count: 992 physics-based features derived from 80 base signals (not 512). Precision matters for technical credibility.
Name the model architecture (MLP) and quantify success: 96% recall, 100% precision, 30-second lead time, 3x timing margin for load shedding.
Explain validation: held-out bus testing and closed-loop simulation confirmation before deployment—these are core to safety-critical ML design.
eval.better_answer: We chose a 10-bus ring topology because a single failure can propagate; that motivated our design. The critical decision was feature engineering: we extracted 992 physics-based features from 80 base signals—grid-wide aggregates, ring-adjacent imbalances, lags, and rolling statistics—to capture grid dynamics. We trained an MLP that achieved 96% recall, 100% precision, and a 30-second lead time, giving us a 3x safety margin before load shedding was needed. We validated everything in closed-loop simulation: all 10 buses survived after shedding the affected bus to 30% load. That validation step was essential—it proved the model worked end-to-end in realistic conditions.

review.headline: You have strong real work behind you (a 10-bus DC grid early-warning pipeline), but in these two answers it came across as vague and rushed, with a wrong feature count and few of the numbers that make the project credible.

content.summary: Your motivation in Q1 (using AI so people face less danger around high-voltage grids) is genuine and relevant, but it stayed generic and never mentioned your actual project or results. In Q2 you gave the right skeleton (ring topology, feature engineering, neural network, early warning, cutting power to the affected bus), but you said '512 features' where your resume says 992 from 80 base signals. You also left out the MLP, the 96% recall, zero false alarms, 30-second lead time, and the held-out-bus and closed-loop validation, which are exactly what this role screens for. Your reason for the ring topology ('if the grid fails, the whole grid is gonna fail') was unclear.

delivery.summary: You spoke at about 204 words/min, well above the 120-165 target, with filler words at 12.6/min against a benchmark of under 3/min ('like' x11, um/uh x8). Fillers roughly doubled from Q1 (7.5/min) to Q2 (15.4/min) as the question got more technical, and several Q2 sentences restarted mid-thought ('the future engineering, like, extracting the engineering...'). Vocal variation was low (0.43), so key results would not stand out even if you stated them. On the positive side, you had no long pauses and no hedging.

body_language.summary: You stayed fully in frame and never sat too close. Eye contact was in a natural range for Q1 (75%) but dropped to 58% in Q2 with one look-away of about 2 seconds, a tendency to look away when searching for technical detail. The very low final-minute figure (8%) likely reflects a short closing segment, so it should not be over-read. Head motion averaged 12.6 deg/s, roughly double the ~6 deg/s that reads as steady, so you may be moving your head a lot while talking.

strengths: Your Q1 motivation is concrete and human: reducing people's exposure to dangerous high-voltage work and helping grids avoid collapse, which fits the role's mission.

In Q2 you described the correct end-to-end logic: topology choice, feature engineering, a neural network predicting bus collapse, and cutting power to the affected bus. This matches your resume and the core of the job.
You started promptly, stayed in frame, and had no hedging or long pauses, so the basics of presence are sound.
